CHAPTER 4: THE MARKET ECONOMY
(Study the price controls section of Chapter 7 alongside this chapter.)

TYPES OF DEMAND
- Individual demand: the quantity demanded of a good/service by individual consumers at different prices.
- Market demand: the aggregate (total) quantity demanded by all consumers in a market at different prices.
- Derived demand: demand for a good not for its own sake but for its use in producing other goods. Applies to factors of production (land, labour, capital, enterprise). E.g. more demand for cars raises demand for steel.
- Composite demand: a good with more than one use; more demand for one product can reduce supply of another. E.g. milk for yogurt and ice cream; oil for fuels and plastics.
- Joint demand: complementary goods bought and consumed together, e.g. fish and chips.
- Effective demand: demand backed by purchasing power - the willingness AND ability to buy at different prices.
- Demand schedule: a table of quantities demanded at different prices.
- Headphones market demand schedule (Table 4.1): 10 euro - 20,000; 8 euro - 30,000; 6 euro - 50,000; 4 euro - 80,000; 2 euro - 120,000.

THE LAW OF DEMAND
- As price falls, quantity demanded rises; as price rises, quantity demanded falls. A negative (inverse) relationship.
- Demand curve (in words): price on the vertical axis, quantity on the horizontal; slopes downward from left to right (negative slope). Its steepness reflects consumers' price sensitivity (price elasticity, Chapter 5).

EXCEPTIONS TO THE LAW OF DEMAND (positive relationship between price and quantity demanded)
- 1. Snob goods / Veblen goods: bought because the high price makes them attractive as status symbols (conspicuous consumption - term from economist Thorstein Veblen). E.g. a handbag rising from 10,000 to 20,000 euro could see demand rise; falling to 5,000 euro could see demand fall as it loses status but is still too dear for most. Rolex watches.
- 2. Giffen goods (Sir Robert Giffen): a necessity; few/no substitutes; bought by those on low incomes; when its price rises, demand rises. E.g. bread in poor communities in the late 1800s - when bread price rose, people cut luxuries like meat and spent more on bread.
- 3. Goods affected by expectations: when property prices fall in a recession, buyers may wait for further falls, so quantity demanded falls; when prices rise, people buy now expecting further rises. Stocks and shares are another example.

MOVEMENT ALONG VS SHIFT OF THE DEMAND CURVE
- Movement along the demand curve: caused ONLY by a change in the price of the good itself. Called a change in quantity demanded. E.g. headphones from 10 euro to 2 euro: from point A (20,000) to point B (120,000).
- Shift (movement) of the demand curve: a change in demand at any given price. Left = demand falls at each price (D1 to D2, Q1 to Q2 lower). Right = demand rises at each price.

FACTORS THAT SHIFT THE DEMAND CURVE
- 1. Change in income:
- Normal good: demand rises when income rises and falls when income falls. Most goods.
- Inferior good: demand falls when income rises and rises when income falls. E.g. tinned meat, supermarket own-brand products (own-brand noodles). 'Inferior' compared with a dearer substitute (market-leading brand).
- Curve moves LEFT if: normal good and income falls, OR inferior good and income rises.
- Curve moves RIGHT if: normal good and income rises, OR inferior good and income falls (e.g. own brands more popular in a recession).
- 2. Price of substitutes (goods that satisfy the same need, e.g. butter and margarine, Pepsi and Coca-Cola):
- Fall in price of a substitute - demand for the good falls (left). E.g. cheaper margarine, less butter demanded.
- Rise in price of a substitute - demand for the good rises (right).
- 3. Price of complements (goods bought together, joint demand, e.g. diesel and diesel-engine cars):
- Rise in price of a complement - demand falls (left). E.g. dearer diesel (carbon tax) cuts demand for diesel cars.
- Fall in price of a complement - demand rises (right).
- 4. Advertising, tastes/preferences, publicity:
- Negative publicity, bad reviews (e.g. Trustpilot), tastes moving away - left. E.g. beef (emissions publicity); printed newspapers (online news); terrestrial TV (streaming like Netflix, Amazon Prime).
- Positive publicity, influencer endorsements, ads, tastes moving towards - right. E.g. fitness watches (health-conscious); veganism; face masks and hand sanitiser in 2020 (WHO and government advice).
- 5. Expectations about future price, availability and income:
- Expect lower prices, abundant supply or lower income - left. E.g. people delay buying electronics before Black Friday/Cyber Monday; pessimism about higher direct taxes, pay cuts or job losses.
- Expect higher prices, shortages or higher income - right. E.g. toilet paper stockpiling and panic-buying of food early in Covid-19; optimism about lower taxes or pay rises.
- 6. Population/market size: fall (more emigration, less immigration) - left, e.g. less demand for public transport; rise - right.
- 7. Availability of credit and interest rates: less lending/dearer credit - left for property (mortgages) and new cars (PCP finance, car loans); more lending/cheaper credit - right (e.g. cheap credit in the Celtic Tiger). Banks have tended to lend too much in booms and too little in recessions.
- 8. Unplanned factors: negative - Covid-19 cut demand for air travel, hotel breaks, petrol/diesel, takeaway coffees; poor summer weather cuts demand for ice cream, barbecues, sun cream. Positive - Covid-19 raised demand for face masks, PPE, ventilators, sanitiser, wipes; good weather raises ice cream demand.

SUPPLY
- Individual supply: quantity supplied by individual suppliers at different prices.
- Market supply: aggregate (total) quantity supplied by all suppliers at different prices.
- Supply schedule: table of quantities supplied at different prices.
- Headphones supply schedule (Table 4.2): 10 euro - 120,000; 8 euro - 80,000; 6 euro - 50,000; 4 euro - 30,000; 2 euro - 20,000.
- Law of Supply: as price rises, quantity supplied rises; as price falls, quantity supplied falls. Positive relationship (higher price is more profitable). Supply curve slopes upward.

EXCEPTIONS TO THE LAW OF SUPPLY
- 1. Supply is fixed: e.g. a concert venue with 1,000 seats supplies 1,000 tickets at 10, 20, 30, 40 or 50 euro. Supply curve is vertical - perfectly inelastic. Also a seller of perishable goods near their sell-by date (fish, fruit, vegetables, flowers) - a fixed amount to sell; a low price is better than disposing of unsold stock.
- 2. Supplier close to maximum capacity: can raise output at first (e.g. a ventilator factory going from five to seven days a week in Covid-19), but eventually cannot (Table 4.4: 1,000 euro - 100; 2,000 - 200; 3,000 - 300; 4,000 - 400; 5,000 and 6,000 - still 400). Curve slopes up then becomes vertical at 400.
- 3. Labour supply when a trade union negotiates a minimum wage (covered later).

MOVEMENT ALONG VS SHIFT OF THE SUPPLY CURVE
- Movement along: ONLY a change in the good's own price; a change in quantity supplied. E.g. headphones 2 euro to 10 euro: point A to point B.
- Shift: a change in supply at any given price. Left = supply falls; right = supply rises.

FACTORS THAT SHIFT THE SUPPLY CURVE
- 1. Costs of production (wages, raw materials, energy): rise - left; fall - right. E.g. a bakery worker's pay rising from 1,000 to 2,000 euro a month leaves less for ingredients. A TY mini-company with 100 euro finding ingredient prices halved can make twice as many cakes.
- 2. Price of related goods (other goods the supplier could make with its resources): farmer with carrots and parsnips - rise in carrot price reduces parsnip supply (left) as land moves to carrots; fall in carrot price increases parsnip supply (right).
- 3. Unplanned factors (outside the firm's control): negative - droughts, storms, strikes, delays at ports and transport disruption (e.g. Covid-19 and Brexit uncertainty disrupted raw materials for UK car plants, suspending production at end of 2020); positive - ideal weather increases agricultural supply.
- 4. Government/EU subsidies: a subsidy is a payment to a supplier covering some production costs (lump sum towards fixed costs or per-unit towards variable costs). Common in agriculture to encourage production and raise farm incomes. Rise in subsidies - right; fall - left.
- 5. Number of sellers: fall - left (fewer music stores, fewer CDs); rise - right (more coffee shops, more coffee).
- 6. Advances in technology: shift supply right. New methods, machinery, faster computers and broadband raise efficiency and productivity. Communications technology (internet, 5G, mobile devices) has increased globalisation.

MARKET EQUILIBRIUM AND THE PRICE MECHANISM
- Market: where buyers and sellers come together; shown by drawing demand and supply on one diagram.
- Headphones (Table 4.5): equilibrium price (Pe) 6 euro, equilibrium quantity (Qe) 50,000, where Qd = Qs.
- Equilibrium price: the price at which everything supplied is demanded; no unsold stock (excess supply) and no unsatisfied customers (excess demand). Equilibrium is a point from which there is no tendency to change.
- Excess supply (surplus): at 10 euro, 120,000 supplied but 20,000 demanded - 100,000 unsold. Suppliers cut price; more is demanded and less supplied until Qd = Qs.
- Excess demand: at 2 euro, 20,000 supplied but 120,000 demanded - 100,000 unsatisfied customers. Price rises; more supplied and less demanded until Qd = Qs.

THREE FUNCTIONS OF THE PRICE MECHANISM (TABLE 4.6)
- 1. Signalling: prices signal market conditions. Too high - unsold stock - signal to cut price. Too low - shortages - signal to raise price.
- 2. Rationing: a price rise due to scarcity discourages consumption, conserving resources (e.g. dearer oil makes people careful with fuel). High prices deter some buyers, so only those willing and able to pay remain (e.g. high Dublin rents ration scarce rental properties).
- 3. Allocating resources: e.g. a seller of wired and Bluetooth headphones cuts the price of unsold wired ones (less profit) and raises the price of popular Bluetooth ones (more profit), so moves more resources to Bluetooth.

WORKED EXAMPLE: CHANGES IN EQUILIBRIUM (JEANS MARKET)
- Downturn cuts real incomes: demand shifts left; price falls P1 to P2; quantity falls Q1 to Q2.
- Fall in price of cotton (input): supply shifts right; price falls; quantity rises.
- Influencer endorsement: demand shifts right; price rises; quantity rises.
- Competitor cuts prices (substitute cheaper): demand shifts left; price falls; quantity falls.

IMPACT OF TECHNOLOGY ON THE MARKET ECONOMY
- Since the 1990s communications technology (internet, smartphones, 5G) has advanced globalisation and changed how consumers buy and suppliers sell.
- Aviation: online flight booking. Tourist accommodation: booking.com, Airbnb, trivago.
- Online vs high street shopping: more choice and variety from suppliers worldwide, possibly at the expense of local retailers without an online presence (Amazon - biggest online retailer; Boohoo.com).
- Online gambling: 24/7 access to a larger market; gambling addiction a major problem.
- Advertising: targeted social media ads using user data; influencers shape tastes; less revenue for printed newspapers.
- Information: reviews (Tripadvisor, Trustpilot), price tracking (camelcamelcamel.com), comparison sites (bonkers.ie) - puts downward pressure on prices.
- Banking: automated and online; less cash and cheques; split bills with Revolut; cashless banks (KBC 'hubs').
- Education: online learning after Covid-19 - universities can enrol more without expanding facilities; more accessible.
- Streaming (Netflix, Amazon Prime) at the expense of terrestrial TV; free online news (thejournal.ie) replacing printed newspapers.

CASE STUDY: IRISH RESIDENTIAL PROPERTY MARKET
- Big price swings since the late 1990s; strong tradition of ownership. Prices rose late 1990s-2007, fell 2008-2012, rose 2013-2020.
- 'Walford', Shrewsbury Road, Dublin: bought for 58 million euro in 2005, sold for 14.25 million euro in 2016.
- Reasons for RISING prices (more demand, limited supply in some places): 1. rising incomes and employment (FDI, exports); 2. rising population (less emigration, more immigration, natural increase); 3. expectations of higher prices ('buy now before it's dearer') - an exception to the Law of Demand; 4. investor demand (rising rents, cheap credit); 5. access to credit (cheap in the Celtic Tiger; slowly returning from 2012/2013); 6. Help to Buy scheme (2016, enhanced mid-2020): first-time buyers can get a tax rebate of 10% of the price up to 30,000 euro, raising demand and prices of new homes; 7. supply of new homes slow to rise in 2012-2020.
- Reasons for FALLING prices 2008-2012 (less demand, excess supply): 1. falling incomes and unemployment, high direct taxes, pay cuts; 2. falling population (more emigration, less immigration); 3. expectations of lower prices - buyers wait, construction fell (Law of Supply); 4. less investor demand (lower rents, higher taxes on rent, higher mortgage rates); 5. less credit, higher interest rates, lenders left (Danske Bank, Bank of Scotland (Ireland)).

GOVERNMENT VS CENTRAL BANK (CONFLICTING POLICIES)
- The Central Bank is independent of the government.
- Government: wants more homes built, so pursues policies that raise new home prices (Law of Supply), e.g. Help to Buy lets first-time buyers fund bigger deposits and pay more.
- Central Bank: as regulator, wants to prevent a repeat of past problems by limiting borrowing, protecting banks and borrowers.
- 2016 Central Bank mortgage rules: borrow max 3.5 times gross income; first-time buyers need a 10% deposit; non-first-time buyers 20%; investors (landlords) 30%.
- Positive implications (Table 4.9): banks protected if prices fall (e.g. a landlord defaults and price falls 30% - bank repossesses, sells and clears loan without loss); taxpayers less likely to bail out banks (last bailout cost 64 billion euro).
- Negative implications: buyers save longer and rent longer, pushing up rents; limited borrowing means potentially lower prices, so builders build fewer homes (Law of Supply), worsening the housing crisis.

THE PRIVATE RENTAL MARKET
- Supply fell because: 1. landlords left (high taxes on rental income, strict quality regulations, property tax); 2. owners let properties to tourists on Airbnb up to Covid-19 (especially Galway, Cork, Dublin); 3. builders slow to build homes - commercial property (Dublin offices, hotels, student accommodation) was more lucrative up to 2020.
- Demand rose because: 1. rising population in some areas (natural increase, returning emigrants, immigration, rising employment, more third-level students); 2. 2016 mortgage rules forced people to rent longer while saving; 3. shortage of social housing - government used the Housing Assistance Payment (HAP) to subsidise private rents rather than build, raising rental demand and rents.
- Rent controls: speculation in late 2015 led landlords to raise rents before new laws; November 2015 restrictions came after many rents had risen - the threat of freezes caused rents to rise.
- Rent Pressure Zones (RPZs) (list at rtb.ie): rent increases limited to 4% a year up to 2021; landlords outside RPZs raised rents in case they were added later. Since 2021, increases capped in line with inflation.

PRICE CEILING (RENT CEILING)
- Price ceiling: a maximum price set below the equilibrium price, above which suppliers cannot charge.
- Table 4.10 rents: 2,000 euro Qd 20,000 Qs 50,000; 1,750 - 25,000/45,000; 1,500 - 30,000/40,000; 1,250 - 35,000/35,000; 1,000 - 40,000/30,000; 750 - 45,000/25,000; 250 - 50,000/15,000.
- Equilibrium rent 1,250 euro, 35,000 properties. Price ceiling (Pmax) of 750 euro.
- Consequences: 1. landlords withdraw; supply falls to 25,000, demand rises to 45,000 - excess demand of 20,000 tenants; 2. 'cash' rents in the hidden economy; 3. extra charges (parking space, garden access); 4. lower quality as less money to maintain properties; 5. lower tax on rental income, so less government current revenue.

CONSUMER SURPLUS AND PRODUCER SURPLUS
- Table 4.11: 10 euro Qd 50 Qs 10; 20 - 40/20; 30 - 30/30; 40 - 20/40; 50 - 10/50; 60 - 0/60. Equilibrium 30 euro, 30 units (each consumer buys one unit).
- Consumer surplus: the difference between what a consumer would be willing to pay rather than do without and what they actually pay. E.g. the 10th customer would pay 50 euro, pays 30 - surplus 20 euro; 20th customer would pay 40 - surplus 10 euro.
- Total consumer surplus = area of triangle below the demand curve and above the equilibrium price = 1/2 x 30 x (60 - 30) = 450 euro.
- Producer surplus: the difference between the price the seller would have accepted and the price actually received. E.g. 10th unit would be sold for 10, receives 30 - surplus 20; 20th unit - surplus 10.
- Total producer surplus = area of triangle above the supply curve and below the equilibrium price = 1/2 x 30 x 30 = 450 euro.
- Using consumer surplus: Example 1 - concert venue charges 50 euro, but some loyal fans would pay 80; offering an 80 euro option with extras (advance purchase, seats near the stage, meet and greet, VIP package) extracts the extra 30 euro. Example 2 - Aer Lingus Shannon-London: four prices for the same flight (base e.g. 45.99 euro) with extras such as carry-on and checked bags, seat selection, priority boarding, lounge access and flexible bookings. (Price discrimination in Chapter 8.)

rows.prompt: What is effective demand?
options: Demand backed by the willingness and ability to pay
Demand for a good used to make another
Total demand from all consumers in a market
rows.explanation: Effective demand is supported by purchasing power.

rows.prompt: Rising demand for cars raises demand for steel. What type of demand is this?
rows.explanation: Steel is demanded for its use in making cars, not for its own sake.

rows.prompt: Milk is used to make both yogurt and ice cream. What type of demand is this?
rows.explanation: A good with more than one use is in composite demand.

rows.prompt: What does the Law of Demand state?
options: As price falls, quantity supplied rises
As price rises, quantity demanded rises
As price falls, quantity demanded rises
rows.explanation: There is a negative (inverse) relationship between price and quantity demanded.

rows.prompt: Which is a feature of a Giffen good?
options: It is a luxury bought as a status symbol
It is a necessity bought by people on low incomes
Demand falls when its price rises
rows.explanation: Giffen goods are necessities with few substitutes, bought by low-income people, whose demand rises with price.

rows.prompt: Why might demand for a 20,000 euro handbag fall if its price falls to 5,000 euro?
options: It loses appeal as a status symbol
rows.explanation: Veblen goods are bought partly because they are expensive (conspicuous consumption).

rows.prompt: What is the ONLY factor that causes a movement along a demand curve?
options: A change in the price of substitutes
A change in the price of the good itself
rows.explanation: All other factors shift the curve; only own price moves along it.

rows.prompt: Demand for an inferior good rises when what happens?
options: The price of a complement rises
rows.explanation: Demand for inferior goods (e.g. own-brand noodles) rises when incomes fall.

rows.prompt: The price of margarine falls. What happens to the demand curve for butter?
options: There is a movement along it
rows.explanation: Margarine is a substitute; when it gets cheaper, some consumers switch away from butter.

rows.prompt: A carbon tax raises the price of diesel. What happens to demand for diesel-engine cars?
options: It rises, shifting the curve right
It falls, shifting the curve left
rows.explanation: Diesel and diesel cars are complements, so a dearer complement reduces demand.

rows.prompt: Why did demand for electronics fall in the weeks before Black Friday?
options: Consumers expected lower prices in the sales
rows.explanation: Expectations of lower future prices reduce demand at current prices.

rows.prompt: Banks reduce lending and raise interest rates. Which demand curves shift left according to the chapter?
rows.explanation: Property depends on mortgages and new cars on PCP finance and car loans.

rows.prompt: What does the Law of Supply state?
options: As price rises, quantity supplied falls
As price rises, quantity demanded falls
As price rises, quantity supplied rises
rows.explanation: There is a positive relationship between price and quantity supplied.

rows.prompt: A concert venue has 1,000 seats. What shape is the supply curve for tickets?
rows.explanation: Supply is fixed at 1,000 whatever the price.

rows.prompt: Why might a fish seller near the sell-by date sell a fixed amount even at a low price?
options: The government sets a minimum price
A low price is better than disposing of unsold stock
rows.explanation: With perishable goods the seller has a fixed amount and prefers a low price to waste.

rows.prompt: Workers at a bottling plant get a big pay rise. What happens to supply?
options: There is a movement along the curve
rows.explanation: Higher costs of production mean less can be produced, so supply falls at each price.

rows.prompt: A farmer grows carrots and parsnips. The price of carrots rises. What happens to the supply of parsnips?
options: It falls as land moves to carrots
It rises as parsnips become dearer
rows.explanation: Resources are reallocated to the now relatively more profitable carrots.

rows.prompt: What is a subsidy?
options: A tax on each unit sold
A maximum price set by government
A payment to a supplier covering some production costs
A loan from a bank to a firm
rows.explanation: Subsidies incentivise producers to increase output, shifting supply right.

rows.prompt: Which would shift the supply curve to the right?
rows.explanation: Better technology increases efficiency and productivity; the others reduce supply.

rows.prompt: What is the equilibrium price?
options: The highest price consumers will pay
The price set by the government
The lowest price sellers will accept
The price where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
rows.explanation: At equilibrium there is no excess supply or excess demand.

rows.prompt: Headphones: at 10 euro, Qd = 20,000 and Qs = 120,000. What exists?
rows.explanation: 120,000 minus 20,000 is 100,000 units of unsold stock.

rows.prompt: Using Table 4.7, Qd = Qs = 800 iPhones. What is the equilibrium price?
rows.explanation: At 600 euro both quantity demanded and supplied are 800.

rows.prompt: High Dublin rents deter many people so only those willing and able to pay remain. Which function of the price mechanism is this?
rows.explanation: Higher prices ration scarce goods among those willing and able to pay.

rows.prompt: A fall in the price of cotton affects the jeans market. What happens to equilibrium?
rows.explanation: Lower costs shift supply right, lowering price and raising quantity.

rows.prompt: According to the chapter, how do price comparison websites like bonkers.ie affect prices?
options: They put downward pressure on prices
They have no effect on prices
rows.explanation: Easier access to price information puts downward pressure on prices.

rows.prompt: Under the Help to Buy scheme, what was the maximum tax rebate for a first-time buyer?
rows.explanation: First-time buyers could get 10% of the price back, up to 30,000 euro.

rows.prompt: Under the 2016 Central Bank rules, how much can people borrow?
rows.explanation: Borrowers can borrow only 3.5 times their gross income.

rows.prompt: What deposit must investors (landlords) have under the Central Bank rules?
rows.explanation: First-time buyers need 10%, other buyers 20% and investors 30%.

rows.prompt: How do the government and Central Bank conflict in the property market?
options: The government cuts prices; the Bank raises lending
Both aim to lower property prices
The government raises prices to boost building; the Bank limits borrowing
Both aim to raise mortgage lending
rows.explanation: Help to Buy pushes prices up to encourage building, while lending rules restrict what buyers can pay.

rows.prompt: What were rent increases limited to in Rent Pressure Zones up to 2021?
rows.explanation: Up to 2021 RPZ rent increases were capped at 4% a year; since 2021, in line with inflation.

rows.prompt: Equilibrium rent is 1,250 euro. A 750 euro ceiling gives Qd 45,000 and Qs 25,000. What results?
rows.explanation: 45,000 minus 25,000 means 20,000 people cannot find a property.

rows.prompt: A customer would pay 50 euro but the market price is 30 euro. What is their consumer surplus?
rows.explanation: Consumer surplus is what they would pay minus what they pay: 50 - 30 = 20 euro.

rows.prompt: Explain derived demand, composite demand and joint demand, with an example of each.
rows.model_answer: Derived demand is demand for something for its use in making other goods, e.g. steel for cars. Composite demand is where a good has more than one use, e.g. milk for yogurt and ice cream. Joint demand is for complements consumed together, e.g. fish and chips.

rows.prompt: Explain, with examples, a Giffen good and a snob (Veblen) good.
rows.model_answer: A Giffen good is a necessity with few substitutes, bought by low-income people, whose demand rises when its price rises, e.g. bread in poor communities in the late 1800s. A snob/Veblen good is bought because its high price makes it a status symbol (conspicuous consumption), e.g. a high-end handbag or Rolex watch.

rows.prompt: Explain the difference between a normal good and an inferior good.
rows.model_answer: Demand for a normal good rises when income rises and falls when income falls; most goods are normal. Demand for an inferior good falls when income rises and rises when income falls, e.g. tinned meat or own-brand noodles, which become more popular in a recession.

rows.prompt: Describe in words the supply curve of a firm close to maximum capacity.
rows.model_answer: With price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal, the curve slopes upward at first as the firm raises output in response to higher prices (e.g. from 100 to 400 units). Once maximum capacity is reached (400 units), the curve becomes vertical because output cannot rise further, however high the price.

rows.prompt: State and explain the three functions of the price mechanism.
rows.model_answer: Signalling: prices signal market conditions - unsold stock tells sellers to cut prices; shortages tell them to raise prices. Rationing: higher prices reduce consumption of scarce goods and leave only those willing and able to pay. Allocating resources: sellers move resources to more profitable goods, e.g. from wired to Bluetooth headphones.

rows.prompt: State four of the 2016 Central Bank mortgage lending rules.
rows.model_answer: Borrowers can borrow only 3.5 times gross income. First-time buyers need a 10% deposit. Non-first-time buyers need a 20% deposit. Investors (landlords) need a 30% deposit.

rows.prompt: Explain three reasons why rents rose in the private rental market.
rows.model_answer: Supply fell as landlords left due to high taxes on rental income, strict regulations and property tax, and as owners let to tourists on Airbnb. Demand rose with population growth and because the 2016 mortgage rules forced people to rent for longer. The government used HAP to place social housing tenants in private rentals, increasing demand further.

rows.prompt: Explain consumer surplus and how an airline can use it to raise revenue.
rows.model_answer: Consumer surplus is the difference between what a consumer would be willing to pay and what they actually pay. Some passengers would pay more than the basic fare, so Aer Lingus offers dearer packages with extras such as checked bags, seat selection, priority boarding, lounge access and flexibility, extracting some of that surplus.

rows.prompt: Explain, with the aid of a diagram, how the price mechanism brings a market to equilibrium. Refer to excess supply and excess demand. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Diagram (described): price on the vertical axis, quantity on the horizontal; a downward-sloping demand curve and an upward-sloping supply curve cross at the equilibrium price (Pe 6 euro) and quantity (Qe 50,000) for headphones. Equilibrium price is the price at which everything supplied is demanded - no unsold stock and no unsatisfied customers. Excess supply: at 10 euro, 120,000 are supplied but only 20,000 demanded, leaving 100,000 unsold. Suppliers take this as a signal to cut price; as price falls, quantity demanded rises (Law of Demand) and quantity supplied falls (Law of Supply) until Qd = Qs. Excess demand: at 2 euro, 120,000 are demanded but only 20,000 supplied, leaving 100,000 unsatisfied customers. Suppliers raise price; quantity supplied rises and quantity demanded falls until Qd = Qs. Price acts as a signal to buyers and sellers until equilibrium is reached.
rows.marking_scheme: Diagram: 6 marks (axes 2, curves 2, Pe/Qe labelled 2). Equilibrium explained: 4 marks. Excess supply: 5 marks (2 + 3). Excess demand: 5 marks (2 + 3).

rows.prompt: The demand curve for fitness watches has shifted to the right. State and explain five factors that could cause this. (25 marks)
rows.model_answer: 1. Rise in income: fitness watches are a normal good, so higher incomes increase demand at each price. 2. Rise in the price of a substitute: if rival devices get dearer, consumers switch to fitness watches. 3. Fall in the price of a complement: cheaper complementary goods make buying the watch more attractive. 4. Positive publicity and changing tastes: consumers are becoming more health-conscious and influencer endorsements and advertising increase demand. 5. Expectations: if consumers expect higher future prices or shortages, or are optimistic about future income (e.g. lower direct taxes or pay rises), they buy now. Other factors: a rise in population/market size, and greater availability of cheap credit.
rows.marking_scheme: 5 points x 5 marks (2 marks statement + 3 marks explanation).

rows.prompt: The government introduces a rent ceiling below the equilibrium rent. Explain, with the aid of a diagram, the effects on the private rental market. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Diagram (described): rent on the vertical axis, quantity of properties on the horizontal. Demand slopes down and supply slopes up, crossing at equilibrium rent of 1,250 euro and 35,000 properties. A horizontal line at 750 euro (Pmax) below equilibrium meets supply at 25,000 and demand at 45,000. Effects: 1. Excess demand - landlords withdraw so supply falls to 25,000 while demand rises to 45,000, leaving 20,000 people unable to find a home. 2. Hidden economy - some landlords rent for cash at higher rents to avoid the ceiling. 3. Extra charges - landlords add charges for parking or garden access. 4. Lower quality - less income to maintain properties. 5. Lower tax revenue - less rental income means less government current revenue.
rows.marking_scheme: Diagram: 5 marks (curves, equilibrium, ceiling below equilibrium, shortage shown). Effects: 3 points x 5 marks (2 marks statement + 3 marks explanation).

rows.prompt: Discuss the positive and negative implications of the Central Bank's 2016 restrictions on mortgage lending. (15 marks)
rows.model_answer: Positive: 1. Banks are protected from large property price falls; e.g. with a 30% deposit, if a landlord defaults and the property falls 30% in value, the bank can repossess, sell and clear the loan without a loss. 2. Taxpayers are less likely to have to bail out banks again, since less risky lending takes place; the last bailout cost 64 billion euro. Negative: 1. Larger deposits and the 3.5 times income limit mean buyers save for longer and rent for longer, pushing up rents. 2. Under the Law of Supply, if buyers can borrow less, prices are potentially lower, so builders build fewer homes, worsening the housing crisis.
rows.marking_scheme: 3 points x 5 marks (2 marks statement + 3 marks explanation), at least one positive and one negative.
